pages.text: The downpour lasted barely ninety minutes, yet brown floodwater surged over the concrete culvert at Zongo Junction. It soaked three bales of wax print in the stall of Fauzia’s mother. Five weeks later, five students at the school, including Selorm’s younger sister, were absent with confirmed malaria. “It is the gutter smell that made them sick,” a trader insisted. Kukua was not sure. From the paved walkway she pointed to a tangled dam of sachet-water rubbers, takeaway packs, and silt wedged across the drain mouth. “People blame only the heavy rain,” Fauzia said quietly, “but look at what held the water back.”

pages.text: In Integrated Science, the class took the problem in two halves. “First, why are heavy storms becoming more common?” their teacher asked, sketching the carbon cycle. “Green plants absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and lock the carbon into wood and soil. When we burn fossil fuels, tyres, and heaps of plastic, and cut down trees, extra greenhouse gases build up. They trap heat in Earth’s atmosphere. No one can blame a single storm on climate change, but a warmer atmosphere makes heavy downpours and heatwaves more likely. Second, most plastics are non-biodegradable. Decomposers in the soil cannot break them down, so a sachet can last for decades, blocking drains and leaving pools of stagnant water.”

pages.text: On Thursday, Municipal Environmental Health Officer Madam Korkor visited to clear up a dangerous misconception. “A choked gutter smells bad, but its smell cannot give you malaria. Neither can drinking dirty water,” she said firmly. “Malaria is caused by a microscopic parasite called Plasmodium. It is spread to people by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. The mosquito is the vector: it carries the parasite from person to person. Now, where does Anopheles breed? In suitable standing-water habitats, which vary among Anopheles species. Not every puddle suits them, but blocked drains can leave standing pools where some mosquitoes may breed. There the eggs hatch into larvae, the larvae become pupae, and adult mosquitoes emerge within one to two weeks.”

pages.text: In Social Studies, Fauzia mapped why dumping persisted around the market. Many people tossed empty sachets into gutters, assuming the rain would wash them “away”. Paved compounds left no bare soil or shade trees to slow the runoff. “There is no ‘away’ in a drainage basin,” Selorm told the class. “Every sachet dropped uphill becomes somebody’s flooded stall and mosquito pool downhill. And clearing silted drains costs the municipal assembly money that could have equipped clinics and school laboratories.”

pages.text: In RME, the trio prepared an appeal for Friday mosque announcements, Sunday church notices, and Saturday communal labour. Fauzia began with her mother’s spoiled cloth. Then she quoted the Islamic teaching that cleanliness is part of faith, and that removing a harmful thing from the public path is an act of charity, sadaqah. Kukua added the Christian call to love your neighbour in deed, and never dump waste that floods a neighbour’s home. Selorm ended with Ghanaian communal tradition: keeping compounds and waterways clean honours both the elders and children not yet born.

pages.text: The students did not burn the collected plastic, because burning releases toxic fumes and greenhouse gases. Instead, the school partnered with the market queens and a local plastic buy-back recycler. Students placed colour-coded bins at the lorry stops: green for biodegradable food peels to compost in the school garden, and yellow mesh cages for non-biodegradable sachets and bottles to sell for recycling. They also planted shade trees along the school boundary to absorb carbon dioxide and slow the runoff. When the next heavy rain fell, the cleared culvert flowed freely, and far fewer stagnant pools were left behind.

activities.question: How do deforestation and open burning of waste disrupt the carbon cycle and worsen climate extremes?
options: Fewer trees absorb CO₂, while burning releases heat-trapping greenhouse gases
Trees release plastic polymers into clouds during photosynthesis
Burning plastics destroys carbon atoms completely so they vanish from Earth

activities.question: What is the exact scientific relationship between choked gutters, mosquitoes, and malaria?
options: Breathing foul air from gutters puts malaria parasites into the lungs
Plasmodium parasites spread through Anopheles mosquitoes in stagnant water
Male houseflies carry malaria from unwashed mangoes into drinking water

activities.question: Why did the students separate plastics for recycling rather than burning them in an open pit?
options: Burning plastics increases oxygen levels in classroom air
Plastic sachets turn into fertile garden compost within two days if buried
Burning plastics releases toxic smoke; recycling keeps drains clear safely

activities.question: Apply it: A classmate says, "I slept near a smelly gutter, so I will get malaria." Which reply is scientifically correct?
options: Yes, the smell carries Plasmodium into the lungs
Infected female Anopheles mosquitoes spread it; use nets and clear water
No, malaria comes only from drinking dirty water

activities.prompt: Put the four stages of complete metamorphosis in the mosquito life cycle in the correct biological order.
items: Larva feeding beneath the water surface
Pupa transforming just below the surface
Adult winged mosquito emerging into the air

activities.definition: Unable to be broken down naturally into harmless substances by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi.
distractors: Able to rot quickly into rich compost within a few weeks
Capable of absorbing carbon dioxide through green chlorophyll

glossary.definition: The continuous natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, plants, animals, soil, oceans, and fuels.
Describing materials such as polythene plastics that microorganisms cannot break down in any useful time, so they persist for decades.
The single-celled protozoan parasite that causes malaria in humans.
An organism, such as the female Anopheles mosquito in malaria, that transmits a pathogen from one host to another.
Nutrient-rich soil conditioner produced when decomposers break down biodegradable organic waste such as plant peels.
